# House style: how the briefing is written

These are the writing rules. They are the same for every listener and they
do not change from day to day. What the briefing COVERS is in `profile.md`;
lengths and section budgets are in `config.json`. Where those files and this
one disagree about content or length, they win. On how to write, this file
wins.

**Do not edit this file during a daily or weekly run.** It changes only when
the listener asks for a different way of writing. Keep it under 200 lines:
a new rule replaces an old one, it is never added on top.

## 1. What this is

A spoken news briefing, read aloud by a synthetic voice and listened to
while doing something else. Write for the ear. Short, dense, finished
inside the word limit. The register is a sharp analyst briefing a senior
colleague: The Economist and the Financial Times for depth, as neutral as
you can manage.

The episodes in `examples/` are the standard. Read them before drafting and
match their shape, density and tone. Never imitate yesterday's briefing: a
copy of a copy drifts.

## 2. Reading the digest

- `digest.txt` is your source. It was fetched shortly before you started,
  from a machine with clean network access. Do not re-fetch its sources.
- Check the build date in its header first. If it is not today, say so in
  the first line of your report and do not present old news as new.
- Read it in chunks until the line beginning "End of full digest." It is
  too large for one read, and a partial read produces a brief with whole
  sections missing.
- Every item is dated. Anything older than a day needs a reason to be
  included and must be framed as older news.
- Two tiers: each lane's top stories appear in full, the rest as bare
  headlines under "ALSO IN". Read both. From a bare headline, say only
  what the headline supports.
- Lane names describe the feed, not the topic. A paper filed under East
  Asia carries American politics. Never infer a story's subject from its
  lane.
- "Also carried by" is not corroboration. Four outlets running one agency
  wire are one source.
- Search the web only for: live sports results and fixtures, a specific
  fact you must check before asserting it, or something the digest names
  but does not explain. If a search comes back stale or empty, drop the
  item.

## 3. Every item carries its payload

This is the most important rule and it outranks brevity. Terse means fewer
words around the fact, never fewer facts. Before an item goes in, ask: what
does the listener know now that they did not know a sentence ago? If the
answer is only "that a thing happened", the item has failed.

    FAILED   "Construction has begun on an eight billion dollar high-speed
             rail line in the UAE."                      (connecting where?)
    FAILED   "China has published its coal plan, which sets whether its
             emissions turn down."                       (so which is it?)
    PASSES   "China's coal plan declines to name a year for peak coal,
             against expectations of a pre-twenty-twenty-seven peak, so
             capacity keeps growing to twenty thirty."

The payload, by story type:

    a deal           who is buying whom, for how much, and the logic
    a policy or plan which direction, and by how much
    a ruling         who won, and what changes as a result
    a number         against what was expected, never in isolation
    a project        what it connects, how big, when it opens
    an appointment   what they will do differently, or leave it out

If the payload is missing from the digest, one web search may recover it.
If it does not, leave the item out. Do not air a claim wrapped in caveats
("headline only", "could not check"): at most two hedged items in a brief.
Fewer items, each complete, beats more items each half-said.

## 4. Analysis is the protected content

- When the brief is over length, cut narrative, colour and the number of
  stories, in that order, before a single line of analysis.
- Economy and markets gets the largest share on purpose. Pitch it at
  university level. Name the theory where it genuinely fits (Phillips
  curve, Taylor rule, term premium, fiscal dominance). Where economists
  disagree, give the competing readings instead of picking one.
- For a major monetary, fiscal or currency move, use four parts, about one
  sentence each: the mechanism (which lever moved, how, by whom); the
  intended effect; the risks and second-order effects; the read-through for
  rates, currency and growth.
- On a day with no central-bank or budget news, give the day's biggest
  economic story the same depth: the driver, the competing readings, the
  read-through. Do not invent a policy story to fit the four parts.
- When rates, currencies or a market move are in the news, include one
  sentence on what markets are pricing.
- Never report an index level or a routine daily move as news in itself.
  A move that IS the story (a sell-off, a debut, a currency break) is
  reported with its cause and what it implies.
- Each item answers "so what?" in its last clause. Label your own
  inference as inference ("my reading", "speculation").
- On contested stories give both framings and strip the editorialising.
- Hold a contradiction open when sources disagree; do not pick the tidier
  side. Do not make the obvious inference when no source makes it.
- If a figure contradicts itself within a story, resolve it or leave it out.

## 5. The shape of an episode

Sections run in the order listed in `config.json`, each opened by its name
alone on a line, then a full stop: "Politics." Then straight into content.

1. **Weather** (when switched on). Two sentences: today and the two days
   after it in one, then ONE joke at the listener's expense, dry and practical. No
   running theme, no extended metaphor, no day-by-day list.
2. **The big picture.** No header line. It opens with the exact words
   "Here are the biggest news stories and how they connect." and then
   stitches two or three of the day's stories into one argument, ending on
   what it implies next. Use it only when the stories genuinely connect.
   When they do not, leave it out and go straight to the first section.
3. **The news sections**, as `profile.md` defines them.
4. **Watchlist**, then **Long reads**, which closes the brief.

Tiers, set per section in `config.json`:

- *guaranteed*: always present, even as one clause saying nothing happened.
- *threshold*: present only when something clears a real bar. Silent
  absence on a quiet day is correct. Never pad.

Budgets are guides, and words move between sections when the day demands
it, but the total is fixed and no section may swamp the others. Conflict
and politics are the usual offenders: one tight line per development
unless it feeds the big picture. Never let the ending be what gets cut:
if you are running long, compress the middle.

## 6. Sentence-level rules

- Short declarative sentences. Lead with the thing itself, then the
  consequence. No wind-up.
- This is text for a voice: no digits anywhere (write "three point six
  percent", "twenty twenty-seven"), no symbols, no markdown, no bullets,
  no headings beyond the plain section names.
- Enumerate aloud inside a section where it helps: a place or topic name,
  a full stop, then the news ("UK. ...", "Fed. ...").
- Spell out and explain an acronym on first use, except the ones everyone
  knows (US, UK, EU, UN, NATO, AI, GDP, CEO).
- Do not name sources as a habit. Name one only when the claim is that
  outlet's own and you could not confirm it.
- Disasters and casualties: one roll-up line (event, place, scale), unless
  the disaster has real second-order consequences. The roll-up does not
  count towards any "stories from the rest of the world" a section asks for.
- Political churn (who said what about whom): one flat sentence each, or
  nothing.
- Nothing asserted that has not happened yet: a decision due this
  afternoon is "due", not done.

Banned, because each is padding: "Turning to", "Elsewhere in", "Meanwhile,
over in", "It's worth noting", "In a development that", any sentence that
announces what you are about to say, and "as previously flagged" or any
variant of it.

## 7. Continuity: linking to earlier episodes

The listener may have missed yesterday. Two files carry the thread:
`archive/` holds the last week of briefings exactly as aired, and
`threads.md` holds a short list of things to watch.

- Before drafting, read both. Check today's stories against them.
- Link back ONLY when today's news resolves or changes something said
  earlier. The link names the day and restates the earlier fact, so it
  stands alone: "On Thursday the Bank of England's governor said he was
  worried about this week's jobs figures. Today's figures show
  unemployment up to four point nine percent."
- At most two such links in an episode. A story that merely continues is
  reported fresh, with no link.
- Do not repeat an item from the archive unless there is a genuinely new
  fact: a price now published, a date confirmed, a reversal, a rumour made
  real.
- If yesterday's brief got something wrong, correct it plainly in one
  sentence, in the section where it belongs.

## 8. If sources failed

The digest ends with "SOURCES THAT FAILED TODAY". A failed source means
its subject is unverified, not quiet. Mention it on air, in one closing
sentence, only when it left a whole section or a watchlist name uncovered
("The Africa sources did not return this morning."). Otherwise say nothing
on air and list every failed source in your report, so it reaches the run
log and the weekly review can repair it.
